posts.title: Knapsack: why not greedy?
posts.author: Student
posts.body: Q: Why can't we sort by value per weight for 0/1 knapsack? A (TA): That greedy rule is optimal for fractional knapsack only. Counterexample: capacity 10, items (weight 6, value 7), (5, 5), (5, 5). Greedy by ratio picks the first item and gets 7; the optimum takes the two 5-weight items for 10.

posts.title: Memoization vs bottom-up

materials.title: COMPSCI 311 Syllabus
pages: COMPSCI 311: Introduction to Algorithms, Fall 2026. Lectures Tuesday and Thursday 1:00-2:15 PM. This course covers the design and analysis of efficient algorithms: asymptotic analysis, greedy algorithms, divide and conquer, dynamic programming, graph algorithms, network flow and NP-completeness. Prerequisites: COMPSCI 187 and COMPSCI 250.

Grading: homework 30% (six assignments, lowest dropped), quizzes 10%, Midterm 1 15%, Midterm 2 15%, final exam 30%. Homework is submitted as a PDF on Gradescope. Late homework is accepted up to 48 hours late with a 10% penalty per day. Quizzes are on Canvas and close at 9 PM on the due date.

Exams: Midterm 1 covers Lectures 1-9 (through dynamic programming). Midterm 2 covers graph algorithms and network flow. The final exam is cumulative. You may bring one double-sided handwritten note sheet to each exam. Regrade requests must be submitted on Gradescope within one week of grades being released.

Collaboration policy: you may discuss homework with classmates but must write up solutions on your own and list your collaborators. Using solutions from previous semesters or online solution sites is not allowed. Office hours are listed on the Canvas calendar; questions go on Piazza.

materials.title: Lecture 5 slides: Greedy Algorithms
pages: Greedy algorithms build a solution one step at a time, always making the choice that looks best right now. They are fast and simple, but only correct for problems with the right structure.

Interval scheduling: given requests with start and finish times, choose the largest set of non-overlapping requests. Greedy rule: always pick the request that finishes earliest, then discard everything that overlaps it.

Why earliest finish time works: the greedy solution 'stays ahead'. After k choices, the greedy k-th request finishes no later than the k-th request of any optimal solution, so greedy can always fit at least as many requests.
Rules that fail: earliest start time, shortest interval, fewest conflicts. Each has a small counterexample. Always test a greedy rule against counterexamples before trying to prove it.

Exchange argument: take an optimal solution that differs from greedy. Swap one of its choices for the greedy choice without making it worse. Repeating the swap turns the optimal solution into the greedy one, so greedy is optimal.

Scheduling to minimize lateness: jobs have lengths and deadlines. Sorting by earliest deadline first minimizes the maximum lateness. Proof by exchange: any inversion of two adjacent jobs can be swapped without increasing lateness.
Running times: interval scheduling and earliest deadline first both take O(n log n) for sorting plus O(n) for the scan.
Summary: greedy needs a proof. Use 'greedy stays ahead' or an exchange argument. When greedy fails (weighted intervals, 0/1 knapsack) we turn to dynamic programming.

materials.title: Lecture 6 slides: Divide and Conquer
pages: Divide and conquer: split the input into parts, solve each part recursively, then combine the answers. Merge sort is the standard example.
Merge sort: split the array in half, sort each half recursively, merge the two sorted halves in linear time. Recurrence T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n), which solves to O(n log n).
Solving recurrences with the recursion tree: each level of the tree does O(n) total work and there are log n levels, giving O(n log n).
The master theorem: for T(n) = aT(n/b) + O(n^d), compare d with log_b a. If d is larger the top level dominates, if smaller the leaves dominate, if equal there is an extra log factor.
Counting inversions: modify merge sort so the merge step counts pairs that are out of order. Still O(n log n).

Closest pair of points in the plane: split by x-coordinate, solve both halves, then check only points within distance delta of the dividing line, sorted by y. Each point needs to be compared with at most 7 neighbors.
Integer multiplication (Karatsuba): three recursive multiplications of half-size numbers instead of four, giving O(n^1.59).
Summary: write the recurrence, solve it with the tree or master theorem, and prove the combine step is correct.

materials.title: Lecture 7 slides
pages: Lecture 7: Dynamic Programming I. Weighted interval scheduling and memoization.
Weighted interval scheduling: each request has a value. We want non-overlapping requests with the largest total value. The greedy earliest-finish rule no longer works once requests have weights.
Sort requests by finish time. Let p(j) be the last request that ends before request j starts. Either the optimal solution uses request j or it does not.
Recurrence: OPT(j) = max(v_j + OPT(p(j)), OPT(j-1)), with OPT(0) = 0. The first option takes request j, the second skips it.
Naive recursion on this recurrence takes exponential time, because the same subproblems are solved again and again. The recursion tree grows like the Fibonacci numbers.
Memoization stores solutions to subproblems so each is solved once. Keep an array M; before computing OPT(j), check whether M[j] is already filled.
With memoization there are only n distinct subproblems and each takes O(1) work once p(j) is known, so the total is O(n log n) including the sort. Memoization trades memory for time.
Bottom-up alternative: fill M[0], M[1], ..., M[n] in order with a loop. Same running time, no recursion, and it is easier to see which earlier entries each step needs.
Recovering the solution: walk back from j = n. If v_j + M[p(j)] >= M[j-1], request j is in the solution; jump to p(j). Otherwise move to j-1.

Recipe for dynamic programming: define the subproblems, write the recurrence, identify base cases, choose an evaluation order, and analyze the running time as (number of subproblems) x (work per subproblem).

materials.title: Lecture 8 slides: Dynamic Programming II
pages: Lecture 8: Dynamic Programming II. Knapsack, longest common subsequence and edit distance.
0/1 knapsack: items with weights w_i and values v_i, capacity W. Subproblem OPT(i, w) = best value using the first i items with capacity w.
Knapsack recurrence: if w_i > w then OPT(i, w) = OPT(i-1, w); otherwise OPT(i, w) = max(OPT(i-1, w), v_i + OPT(i-1, w - w_i)). Base case OPT(0, w) = 0.
Knapsack takes O(nW) time. This is pseudo-polynomial: it depends on the numeric value W, not on the number of bits needed to write W.

Longest common subsequence: for strings X and Y, let L(i, j) be the LCS length of the first i characters of X and the first j characters of Y. If x_i = y_j then L(i, j) = 1 + L(i-1, j-1); otherwise L(i, j) = max(L(i-1, j), L(i, j-1)).
Edit distance: the minimum number of insertions, deletions and substitutions to turn X into Y. D(i, j) = min(D(i-1, j) + 1, D(i, j-1) + 1, D(i-1, j-1) + [x_i != y_j]).
Both LCS and edit distance fill an (m+1) x (n+1) table in O(mn) time. If only the value is needed, keep two rows to use O(n) space.
Common mistakes on homework: forgetting base cases, filling the table in an order that reads entries not yet computed, and analyzing time without counting the subproblems.

materials.title: Lecture 9 slides: Graphs and BFS
pages: Lecture 9: Graphs. Representations, breadth-first search and depth-first search. Graph material is on Midterm 2, not Midterm 1.
Adjacency lists use O(n + m) space and are the default for sparse graphs. Adjacency matrices use O(n^2) space but answer 'is there an edge (u, v)?' in O(1).
Breadth-first search explores the graph in layers: all nodes at distance 1, then distance 2, and so on. It finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs in O(n + m) time.
Depth-first search follows one path as deep as possible before backtracking. It is the basis for finding connected components, cycles and topological orders.
Testing bipartiteness: run BFS and color layers alternately. The graph is bipartite exactly when no edge connects two nodes in the same layer.
Next time: directed graphs, strong connectivity and topological sort.

cues.text: Okay let's get started. Today is divide and conquer. The idea is simple: split the problem, solve the pieces recursively, and then the real work is in how you combine them.
So for merge sort the recurrence is T of n equals two T of n over two plus n. Draw the tree: every level costs n, there are log n levels, so n log n.
The master theorem is just a shortcut for that tree picture. Compare the work at the top with the number of leaves. Don't memorize it without understanding the tree.
Closest pair is the tricky one. After you solve both halves, you only look at a strip of width two delta around the middle line, and each point only checks a constant number of neighbors.
A lot of you lost points on HW 3 because you described the greedy algorithm but never proved it. The proof is the point. Use stays ahead or use an exchange argument.
Exchange argument template: take an optimal solution, find the first place it differs from greedy, swap in the greedy choice, and show the solution is still feasible and no worse.
Now what happens if intervals have weights? Earliest finish time fails. Here's a counterexample: one long interval worth a hundred overlapping two short ones worth one each.
That's exactly why we need dynamic programming next week. Greedy commits too early. DP keeps both options open: take it or skip it.
So we sort by finish time and define p of j, the last interval that finishes before j starts. You can compute all the p values with binary search in n log n.
The recurrence: opt of j is the max of v j plus opt of p of j, or opt of j minus one. Either you take j or you don't. That's the whole idea.
If you just code this recursively it's exponential. Look, opt of j minus two gets computed from both branches, and it keeps doubling. It looks like Fibonacci.
To get the actual set of intervals, not just the value, you trace back through the array. Don't store whole sets in every cell; that blows up the running time.
Today we finish memoization and start the bottom-up view. Remember the array M, one cell per subproblem, initially empty.
So when we memoize, we're trading memory for time. We spend an array of size n, and in exchange each subproblem is solved exactly once instead of exponentially many times.
Bottom-up is the same table filled with a for loop. The order matters: when you compute M of j you need M of p of j and M of j minus one already filled, so go left to right.
For the midterm, I want to see the recurrence in words, the base cases, the order you fill the table, and the running time. That's the template for every DP problem.
Knapsack needs two parameters in the subproblem: which items you've considered and how much capacity is left. One index isn't enough, and that's the most common mistake.
Is n times W polynomial? No. W is a number, and writing it down takes log W bits. So this is pseudo-polynomial. Expect a short answer question on that.
LCS: compare the last characters. If they match, both drop off and you add one. If not, drop one or the other and take the better result.
Edit distance is the same table shape with three options: insert, delete, substitute. Fill row by row; each cell looks up, left and diagonally up-left.
Let's do T of n equals three T of n over two plus n. Three branches, each half the size. The leaves dominate, so it's n to the log base two of three, about n to the one point five nine.
That's Karatsuba. Three multiplications instead of four is the entire trick, and it changes the exponent.
Quiz 4 next week is on recurrences. Practice drawing the tree; it's faster than guessing which case of the master theorem applies.
